newsitem.title: USA: American Airlines, pilots in last-ditch contract talks.
newsitem.headline: American Airlines, pilots in last-ditch contract talks.

text.p: American Airlines and its pilots union opened last-ditch contract talks on Monday to try to avert a nationwide strike set for midnight Friday, with both sides saying their aim was to reach a deal.
If no deal is struck, the pilots union has pledged to close down the carrier, the nation's second largest, carrying 200,000 passengers on 2,200 routes worldwide a day.
After the initial meeting of the two sides, Kenneth Hipp, chairman of the National Mediation Board, which is participating in the talks, called the session "businesslike, very serious."
But he told reporters the first meeting was limited to procedural issues and the sides better defining their positions.

Asked if he expected the talks to head toward an agreement Thursday or Friday, Hipp said, "We would like to get an agreement in the next couple of days." But he added that such a timetable would depend on the parties.
American President Donald Carty told reporters just before the talks began that his negotiators were in Washington "to make a deal."
Carty said the aim of both sides was a strong airline, adding "all we need is a commercial agreement" to reach that goal.
James Sovich, president of the 9,000-member Allied Pilots Association, said separately, "We're here to get a deal also."
A key issue is pay -- the pilots want an increase of 11.5 percent over four years; American has offered 5 percent.
Another is American's plan to add jets to its regional carrier, American Eagle, and allow members of the Eagle union, the Air Lines Pilots Association, to fly them under its lower-pay contract.
American's pilots see that as an effort by American to use the lower-paid commuter pilots to fly routes and jets now being flown by its membership.
But American has said it needs to have the commuter jets flown by the lower-paid pilots to be competitive with its low-cost commuter rivals.

The talks moved to Washington, with federal mediators taking part, after the union's rank-and-file pilots rejected a tentative agreement reached by their negotiators and the failure of reopened talks to resolve differences.
On Friday, members of the Senate Aviation subcommittee urged President Clinton to help mediate the dispute, but the White House indicated it would not step in unless asked by both sides.
The White House said just before the talks began, however, that it would follow the talks "carefully between now and Friday."
But an airline labor expert said "a strike is virually inevitable unless there is major White House intervention."
Joseph Blasi, a professor at Rutgers University's School of Management and Labor Relations, said that if Clinton waits until a strike begins, it would be extremely difficult to resolve.
"The only alternative to a strike is a move by the White House," he said.
In 1993, Clinton ended a five-day strike by American's flight attendants by persuading the airline to agree to binding abitration.

American has called for binding arbitration in the current dispute, now two years old, but the union rejected the idea. Sovich of the pilots' union has said he wanted a deal now and did not want to risk lengthy arbitration for a settlement.

One union official, speaking well before the talks started, said he thought there was a 50-50 chance of a settlement, saying that once the two sides sit down, some new proposals and some creative thinking could emerge.
"That's what you hope for, anyway," he said.
A strike would hit hard at key American Airlines' airports, including its Dallas-Fort Worth home base, as well as Miami, Chicago, Los Angeles, New York and San Juan, Puerto Rico.

American officials say they have arrangements that, in case of a strike, other airlines would accept American's tickets, although there may not be enough seats on the other carriers to carry the thousands of stranded American passengers.

A strike would cost the carrier an estimated $1 billion a month. Last week, American said it was drawing $1 billion from an existing line of credit and had arranged to borrow another $1 billion under a new credit line if needed.
